t: Why fsspec-rs uses explicit protocols and shared traits
x: Why fsspec-rs uses explicit protocols and shared traits fsspec-rs provides Python’s fsspec interface and a Rust filesystem trait. Python applications can select a Rust-backed filesystem through fsspec, while Rust applications can use the native backends without Python. A separate bridge crate lets Rust callers use Python fsspec implementations through the same trait. Explicit protocols preserve compatibility fsspec already assigns file, local, and s3 to established Python implementations. Replacing those registrations globally would make importing fsspec-rs change unrelated application behavior. The file-rs, local-rs, and s3-rs names make backend selection explicit in configuration and allow both implementations to coexist. The classes still inherit from fsspec.spec.AbstractFileSystem. Code written against fsspec operations can therefore select a Rust backend without switching to a different API. Default methods keep native backends small The Rust FileSystem trait follows fsspec’s template-method pattern. A backend implements primitive operations such as listing files, reading metadata, opening files, copying, and removing files. Default trait methods build higher-level operations

t: Why fsspec-rs uses explicit protocols and shared traits
s: Default methods keep native backends small
x: The Rust FileSystem trait follows fsspec’s template-method pattern. A backend implements primitive operations such as listing files, reading metadata, opening files, copying, and removing files. Default trait methods build higher-level operations such as walking, recursive removal, and local transfers from those primitives. This design centralizes shared path and traversal behavior while leaving storage-specific I/O in LocalFs and S3Fs. Default methods may miss backend-specific optimizations, so backends can override them where needed.

t: Why fsspec-rs uses explicit protocols and shared traits
s: The Python bridge is a separate crate
x: The fsspec_rs_bridge crate adapts an installed Python filesystem to the Rust trait, so a Rust component running inside Python can use protocols that have no native Rust implementation. The bridge depends on PyO3 and a Python runtime, while the core fsspec_rs crate does not. Keeping them in separate crates lets standalone Rust applications avoid the Python dependency. Native backends avoid calls into Python; the bridge provides access to Python backends when no native implementation is available.

t: Why fsspec-rs uses explicit protocols and shared traits
x: The local and S3 backends implement the synchronous FileSystem trait. S3 runs async object-store calls through an internal Tokio runtime. Callers use a synchronous interface that matches Python file objects and fsspec, but cannot control async scheduling. The experimental AsyncFileSystem trait defines an async interface without changing the synchronous one. Its status and methods are documented in the Rust reference.

fsspec-rs filesystems fsspec-rs provides Rust-backed filesystems through fsspec classes. Importing fsspec_rs registers the protocols with fsspec: Filesystem Protocols Class Local filesystem file-rs, local-rs fsspec_rs.LocalFileSystem Amazon S3 s3-rs fsspec_rs.S3FileSystem The standard file, local, and s3 registrations remain unchanged. import fsspec import fsspec_rs with fsspec.open("file-rs:///tmp/example.txt", "rb") as f: data = f.read() Local filesystem LocalFileSystem wraps the Rust LocalFs backend, which uses std::fs for local paths. It is marked as a local filesystem (local_file = True) and implements fsspec’s core filesystem operations. from fsspec_rs import LocalFileSystem fs = LocalFileSystem(auto_mkdir=True) fs.pipe_file("/tmp/fsspec-rs/example.txt", b"hello") assert fs.exists("/tmp/fsspec-rs/example.txt") assert fs.isfile("/tmp/fsspec-rs/example.txt") print(fs.info("/tmp/fsspec-rs/example.txt")) Local paths Direct method calls use normal local paths: fs.cat_file("/tmp/fsspec-rs/example.txt") fsspec URLs use file-rs:// or local-rs://: with fsspec.open("local-rs:///tmp/fsspec-rs/example.txt", "rb") as f: print(f.read()) LocalFileSystem._strip_protocol() removes only the Ru

LocalFileSystem wraps the Rust LocalFs backend, which uses std::fs for local paths. It is marked as a local filesystem (local_file = True) and implements fsspec’s core filesystem operations. from fsspec_rs import LocalFileSystem fs = LocalFileSystem(auto_mkdir=True) fs.pipe_file("/tmp/fsspec-rs/example.txt", b"hello") assert fs.exists("/tmp/fsspec-rs/example.txt") assert fs.isfile("/tmp/fsspec-rs/example.txt") print(fs.info("/tmp/fsspec-rs/example.txt"))

Direct method calls use normal local paths: fs.cat_file("/tmp/fsspec-rs/example.txt") fsspec URLs use file-rs:// or local-rs://: with fsspec.open("local-rs:///tmp/fsspec-rs/example.txt", "rb") as f: print(f.read()) LocalFileSystem._strip_protocol() removes only the Rust-specific local protocols. The file:// and local:// protocols still select fsspec’s Python implementation.

Supported modes are rb, wb, ab, and xb, plus the aliases r, w, a, and x at the Rust layer. Python wrappers expose binary file objects that implement read, write, seek, tell, flush, close, readable, writable, and seekable. with fs.open("/tmp/fsspec-rs/out.bin", "wb") as f: f.write(b"payload") with fs.open("/tmp/fsspec-rs/out.bin", "rb") as f: f.seek(2) print(f.read()) auto_mkdir=True creates missing parent directories for write, append, exclusive-create, and copy operations. With the default auto_mkdir=False, the operating system reports an error if a parent directory is missing.

Local filesystem methods delegated to Rust include: Listing and metadata: ls, info, exists, isdir, isfile, size Reads and writes: open, cat_file, pipe_file, head, tail, read_text, write_text, touch Directory operations: mkdir, makedirs, rmdir, walk, find, du Mutation and transfer: rm_file, rm, cp_file, copy, mv, get_file, put_file The cache_type, block_size, and max_blocks options are accepted by open() for API compatibility but do not change local read behavior. Local reads use direct filesystem operations.

S3FileSystem wraps the Rust S3Fs backend, which uses Apache Arrow’s object_store crate and runs its async S3 calls through an embedded Tokio runtime. The Python protocol is s3-rs, so it can coexist with s3fs. from fsspec_rs import S3FileSystem fs = S3FileSystem(bucket="my-bucket", region="us-east-1") fs.pipe_file("reports/hello.txt", b"hello") print(fs.cat_file("reports/hello.txt"))

S3FileSystem is constructed for one bucket. Method calls can use keys within that bucket: fs.ls("reports") fs.info("reports/hello.txt") fsspec URLs include the bucket. _get_kwargs_from_urls() extracts constructor options from the URL: with fsspec.open( "s3-rs://my-bucket/reports/hello.txt", "rb", region="us-east-1", ) as f: print(f.read()) Object names are stored internally without a leading slash. Directory entries are S3 prefixes, not real directories; mkdir() and rmdir() are no-ops.

Credential resolution follows this order: Explicit constructor arguments: key, secret, token, region, endpoint_url, and anon fsspec.config.conf["s3"], including values populated from fsspec config environment variables object_store’s own AWS credential chain, such as environment variables, profiles, and instance or task roles client_kwargs={"endpoint_url": ...} is accepted for compatibility with s3fs. The Rust backend allows plain HTTP when the endpoint starts with http://, as used by local S3-compatible services. fs = S3FileSystem( bucket="benchmark", key="minioadmin", secret="minioadmin", endpoint_url="http://localhost:9000", region="us-east-1", ) Anonymous access is available with anon=True.

S3 reads support optional Rust-side cache strategies through cache_type: cache_type Behavior none Fetch each requested byte range directly. readahead Keep one lookahead window for sequential reads. block Cache fixed-size blocks with LRU eviction. all Fetch the whole object on first read. with fs.open( "large/table.parquet", "rb", cache_type="block", block_size=8 * 1024 * 1024, ) as f: header = f.read(4096) block_size defaults to 4 MiB, and the Rust max_blocks default is 32. The Python file wrapper does not forward max_blocks from open(), so callers cannot change it through that method. Without an explicit cache_type, S3 read mode eagerly loads the whole object into memory. Explicit readahead, block, and none select range-based reads.

S3 methods delegated to Rust include: Listing and metadata: ls, info, exists, isdir, isfile, size Reads and writes: open, cat_file, pipe_file, head, tail, read_text Prefix traversal: walk, find Object mutation: rm_file, rm, cp_file S3 writes buffer object contents in memory before upload. The public API does not support concurrent multipart uploads or signed URLs.

How to use Rust-backed filesystems Replace a local or S3 filesystem with its fsspec-rs equivalent, configure an S3-compatible endpoint, or choose a read cache. Select a backend by protocol Use fsspec to construct a filesystem when an application accepts a protocol: import fsspec import fsspec_rs local = fsspec.filesystem("file-rs", auto_mkdir=True) s3 = fsspec.filesystem("s3-rs", bucket="reports", region="us-east-1") Use direct classes when an application accepts an AbstractFileSystem instance: from fsspec_rs import LocalFileSystem, S3FileSystem local = LocalFileSystem(auto_mkdir=True) s3 = S3FileSystem(bucket="reports", region="us-east-1") Use fsspec URLs Import fsspec_rs before resolving a protocol in environments that do not discover package entry points automatically: import fsspec import fsspec_rs with fsspec.open("file-rs:///tmp/report.txt", "wb") as file: file.write(b"complete\n") with fsspec.open( "s3-rs://reports/2026/summary.txt", "rb", region="us-east-1", ) as file: summary = file.read() Keep file, local, and s3 URLs when you want the existing Python implementations. Omitting cache_type eagerly reads the whole S3 object: with fs.open( "tables/orders.parquet", "rb", cache_type="block", block_size=8 * 1024 * 1024, ) as file: header = file.read(64 * 1024) The Python wrapper uses the Rust default of 32 cached blocks; it does not forward max_blocks. Choose none for direct range fetches, readahead for sequential access, or block for repeated random access. Use all only when you want to fetch the whole object on first read. See the filesystem reference for cache behavior and supported operations.

How to build from source Source builds require Rust, hatch-rs 0.4.3 or newer, and the Cargo license collector. In a source checkout, install the collector before installing the Python package: cargo install cargo-bundle-licenses --version 4.2.0 --locked python -m pip install . For an editable development install, use: python -m pip install -e '.[develop]' If the collector reports missing license texts, check the versioned overrides and source review requirements. See License bundle reference for the wheel bundle’s coverage.

It requires Python and fsspec at runtime: [dependencies] fsspec_rs = "0.1.5" fsspec_rs_bridge = "0.1.5" Resolve a URL and call the filesystem trait: use fsspec_rs::FileSystem; use fsspec_rs_bridge::{url_to_fs, StorageOptions}; let (fs, _) = url_to_fs("memory://", &StorageOptions::new())?; fs.pipe_file("/example.txt", b"hello from Python fsspec")?; assert_eq!(fs.cat_file("/example.txt", None, None)?, b"hello from Python fsspec"); # Ok::<(), fsspec_rs::FsError>(()) For chained URLs, pass options in nested maps keyed by protocol: use fsspec_rs_bridge::{url_to_fs, StorageOptions}; let mut memory = StorageOptions::new(); memory.insert("skip_instance_cache".to_string(), true.into()); let mut options = StorageOptions::new(); options.insert("memory".to_string(), memory.into()); let (fs, path) = url_to_fs("simplecache::memory://bucket/data.csv", &options)?; # Ok::<(), fsspec_rs::FsError>(()) Within this repository’s workspace, use path dependencies ./rust and ./rust/bridge instead of registry versions. See Rust traits for backend primitives and bridge value types.

License bundle reference Wheels include original Cargo dependency license texts in fsspec_rs/licenses/cargo.json. The bundle also includes Cargo dependencies for other targets, beyond those used at runtime by the wheel. It does not cover Python dependencies, native-library notices, or repaired-wheel libraries. The collector does not discover license notices in the r-efi AUTHORS files. Versioned overrides preserve those notices and supply full license terms through licenses.previous. The Cargo override reference records their sources and human review requirements.

Rust traits and types The fsspec_rs crate is independent of Python. The fsspec_rs_bridge crate adapts Python fsspec objects to its synchronous filesystem trait. Most public Rust types are re-exported from the crate root: use fsspec_rs::{ CacheType, FileInfo, FileSystem, FsFile, FsResult, LocalFs, OpenMode, OpenOptions, S3Config, S3Fs, }; Type Purpose FileSystem Synchronous filesystem trait with primitive methods and default helpers. AsyncFileSystem Experimental async mirror of FileSystem; no shipped backend implements it yet. FsFile File-like trait returned by FileSystem::open(). FileInfo Metadata for files, directories, and other entries. OpenMode and OpenOptions Open mode and buffered I/O options. FsError and FsResult<T> Shared error and result types. Cache and CacheType Read cache strategy interface and selector.

LocalFs and S3Fs implement the synchronous FileSystem trait. Backends must implement seven primitive methods and protocol: use fsspec_rs::{FileInfo, FileSystem, FsFile, FsResult, OpenMode, OpenOptions}; struct MyFs; impl FileSystem for MyFs { fn protocol(&self) -> &[&str] { &["myfs"] } fn ls(&self, path: &str, detail: bool) -> FsResult<Vec<FileInfo>> { todo!() } fn rm_file(&self, path: &str) -> FsResult<()> { todo!() } fn cp_file(&self, src: &str, dst: &str) -> FsResult<()> { todo!() } fn open( &self, path: &str, mode: OpenMode, opts: Option<OpenOptions>, ) -> FsResult<Box<dyn FsFile>> { todo!() } fn info(&self, path: &str) -> FsResult<FileInfo> { todo!() } fn mkdir(&self, path: &str, create_parents: bool) -> FsResult<()> { todo!() } fn rmdir(&self, path: &str) -> FsResult<()> { todo!() } } root_marker() defaults to "" and sep() defaults to "/". Backends can override them for local or platform-specific behavior. strip_protocol() and unstrip_protocol() also have defaults and can be overridden when a backend needs bucket-aware or authority-aware paths. The default methods built on those primitives include: Path helpers: strip_protocol, unstrip_protocol, parent Metadata checks: exists

AsyncFileSystem is the experimental async version of FileSystem. Its primitive methods return futures, and its default helpers are async fns. LocalFs and S3Fs implement only the synchronous FileSystem trait. The default async implementation avoids recursive async futures in walk() by using an explicit stack. Method semantics otherwise match FileSystem.

FileSystem::open() returns a file implementing FsFile, which requires Read + Write + Seek + Send. commit() and discard() default to no-ops and are available for buffered writes or future transaction support.

FileInfo is the common metadata value. It stores: name: full path or backend path size: bytes, usually 0 for directories file_type: FileType::File, FileType::Directory, or FileType::Other created and modified: optional SystemTime values extra: backend-specific string metadata such as S3 ETags Convenience constructors are available: let file = FileInfo::file("/tmp/data.bin", 1024); let dir = FileInfo::directory("/tmp"); OpenMode::from_str_mode() accepts rb, wb, ab, xb, and the equivalent single-letter forms. OpenOptions::default() uses a 4 MiB block size, autocommit = true, no explicit cache strategy, and max_blocks = 32.

LocalFs uses std::fs and implements FileSystem. LocalFs::new() starts with auto_mkdir = false. LocalFs::with_auto_mkdir(true) creates missing parent directories during write, append, exclusive-create, and copy operations.

S3Fs wraps object_store::aws::AmazonS3 and runs its async calls through an embedded Tokio runtime to implement the synchronous FileSystem trait. S3Config supports: bucket region endpoint_url access_key_id secret_access_key session_token anon virtual_hosted_style_request Plain HTTP is allowed automatically when endpoint_url starts with http://, which is useful for MinIO and LocalStack.

fsspec_rs_bridge exports PyFsspecFs, url_to_fs, and StorageOptions. It is an rlib using PyO3 and Python fsspec at runtime, with no #[pyclass] exports. url_to_fs(url, options) returns a filesystem adapter and start path. PyFsspecFs::from_protocol(protocol, options) constructs an adapter by protocol. The adapter’s trait protocol is python; source_protocol() reports the wrapped protocol. The bridge initializes and attaches to the Python interpreter internally. PyFsspecFs implements FileSystem and delegates ls, info, open, cat_file, pipe_file, cp_file, rm_file, mkdir, rmdir, get_file, and put_file to Python. Common Python exceptions map to FsError categories. StorageOptions values support nulls, booleans, signed and unsigned integers, floats, strings, lists, and nested maps. Nested maps keyed by protocol configure chained URLs. The Rust guide includes dependency and invocation examples.

The caching layer is used by buffered reads. CacheType::from_str() accepts: Value Strategy none NoCache: every fetch goes to the backend. readahead or read_ahead ReadAheadCache: one lookahead window. block or blockcache BlockCache: fixed-size blocks with LRU eviction. all or bytes AllBytesCache: whole-file cache on first read. Each cache wraps a Fetcher, a FnMut(u64, u64) -> FsResult<Vec<u8>> that retrieves the half-open byte range [start, end) from the backend.

All trait methods return FsResult<T> = Result<T, FsError>. FsError represents filesystem errors with these variants: NotFound PermissionDenied AlreadyExists NotADirectory IsADirectory IoError InvalidArgument NotSupported Other The PyO3 layer maps those variants to Python exceptions such as FileNotFoundError, PermissionError, FileExistsError, NotADirectoryError, IsADirectoryError, ValueError, NotImplementedError, and OSError.

x: Read and write a local file with fsspec-rs Create a file with the Rust-backed local filesystem, then read it through an fsspec URL and inspect its metadata. Before you start Install fsspec-rs in a Python 3.10 or newer environment: python -m pip install fsspec-rs Create the script Create local_demo.py with these imports and a temporary directory: from pathlib import Path from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory import fsspec import fsspec_rs with TemporaryDirectory() as directory: path = Path(directory, "greeting.txt") Write through the Rust-backed filesystem Add this code inside the with block: fs = fsspec.filesystem("file-rs", auto_mkdir=True) fs.pipe_file(str(path), b"hello from Rust\n") print(fs.ls(directory, detail=False)) Run the script: python local_demo.py The listing contains the file you created: ['.../greeting.txt'] Read through an fsspec URL Add this code after the listing, still inside the with block: with fsspec.open(f"file-rs://{path}", "rb") as file: print(file.read().decode().strip()) info = fs.info(str(path)) print(info["type"], info["size"]) Run the script again. fsspec-rs Use Rust-backed local and S3 filesystems through fsspec. Build Status codecov License PyPI fsspec-rs provides Python classes that inherit from fsspec.AbstractFileSystem and delegate core I/O to Rust. The native Rust crate provides shared filesystem traits, local and S3 backends, and read caches. A separate bridge crate adapts Python fsspec implementations for Rust callers. Documentation Start with Read and write a local file for a Python example. Use Rust-backed filesystems covers backend selection, S3 endpoints, and caching. Use the Rust crates covers native and Python-backed Rust access. Look up filesystem behavior, Rust traits and types, or the Python API. Why fsspec-rs uses explicit protocols and shared traits explains the design decisions. For source installations, follow How to build from source. Cargo license overrides The hatch-rs build hook uses license-overrides.json to supply license texts that cargo-bundle-licenses 4.2.0 cannot discover. The file contains only r-efi 5.3.0 and 6.0.0, matched by package name, version, and license identifier. Other dependencies are collected from their source distributions at build time. These overrides require human review before shipping. They do not certify license compliance or change the crates’ declared license choices. Sources Both versions declare MIT OR Apache-2.0 OR LGPL-2.1-or-later. Their AUTHORS files contain the MIT permission text, Apache and LGPL notices, copyright holders, and contributor lists: r-efi 5.3.0 AUTHORS, SHA-256 ff92bed461f50338dd703a9ba9aee496a425957873df1d91192776e4bdf5dda7. r-efi 6.0.0 AUTHORS, SHA-256 d027e91dbc9cdbb2f1190068e498bd6b61cff022b6a032b191021ba658d96111. Each override preserves its version’s complete AUTHORS text. The MIT entry uses that text unchanged. The Apache entry appends the full Apache 2.0 text from the repository’s LICENSE. If the collector cannot find license texts for a new crate version, the build fails until its sources and notices are reviewed and added.
